title: Jurassic Park's computer dinosaurs
hook: The dinosaurs were meant to be stop-motion until one test changed the plan.
peek: Jurassic Park was planned with stop-motion dinosaurs by Phil Tippett. Then artists at Industrial Light & Magic showed Steven Spielberg a computer-made T. rex walking in daylight, and the plan changed. Tippett stayed on, steering the digital dinosaurs with a hand-moved model.
lede: For Jurassic Park, Steven Spielberg planned to combine full-size robotic dinosaurs from Stan Winston's workshop with go-motion, a refined stop-motion technique, by the animator Phil Tippett. At Industrial Light & Magic, a few artists built a computer test, first of a T. rex skeleton and then of a whole animal. When Spielberg saw it, go-motion was dropped.

bullets.text: Tippett is said to have reacted to the news by saying he felt extinct. Spielberg liked the line, and a joke about being extinct made it into the film's script.
Tippett's team kept animating, in a new way. They built a stop-motion-style armature fitted with sensors, so moving the model by hand moved the computer dinosaur on screen.

Stan Winston's full-size animatronic dinosaurs did much of the work, especially up close. The computer-made animals fill only a few minutes of the film, used where a robot could not run or move freely.
The film won the Academy Award for visual effects, shared by Dennis Muren, Stan Winston, Phil Tippett and Michael Lantieri. Its success pushed studios toward computer-made creatures.
